design_detail: Descriptive analysis of service records from the first six months (31 October 2017 to 30 April 2018) of a point-of-care drug-checking pilot run by the British Columbia Centre on Substance Use (BCCSU) with Vancouver Coastal Health at two supervised consumption services (SCS) in downtown Vancouver, where checking was offered two days a week in six-hour shifts at each site. A technician recorded the client's expectation, tested a small portion of the sample by Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectrometry (Bruker ALPHA-Platinum, four reference libraries) and then dissolved it and tested it with a BTNX fentanyl immunoassay strip; fentanyl positivity was generally taken from the strip. Clients were told the results and offered harm-reduction advice. Units are samples (1,714), not people. No confirmatory laboratory testing in this phase (PDF pp. 5–7, 2. Material and methods; PDF p. 7, 3. Results, 1st paragraph). Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist, as the round brief directs for drug-checking data.
can_establish: What share of the samples that a self-selected group of supervised-consumption clients brought for checking in Vancouver in late 2017 and early 2018 tested positive for fentanyl by strip, and contained the expected drug by FTIR, according to what the samples were sold as.
cannot_establish: The make-up of the wider Vancouver drug market (convenience samples), the accuracy of the results (no laboratory confirmation), anything about pills (very few were tested), or what people did after receiving their results (not studied).

sample.recruitment: Convenience samples offered by a self-selected subset of clients of two supervised consumption services in downtown Vancouver, chosen because they had legal authorization for clients to possess controlled substances and a clientele who regularly use opioids, stimulants and other street drugs by injection (PDF p. 5, 2. Material and methods, 1st paragraph; PDF p. 7, 3. Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All samples checked in the period. Nine had no strip result: the text says a strip could not be used for various reasons (PDF p. 7), while Figure 1 labels these 'N/A (declined)' (PDF p. 16).
sample.demographics: Not reported. The number of people who submitted samples, and repeat submissions, are unknown.
sample.selection_effects: Uptake was low (stated as less than 2% of visits) and limited to the hours the service ran; the authors state the samples are not necessarily representative of the broader Vancouver or other illicit drug markets (PDF p. 7, 3. Results, 1st paragraph). People may have submitted several samples, so samples may cluster by person and by batch.

exposure.measurement: FTIR compares sample spectra with reference libraries (2017 versions of the TICTAC ATR-FTIR Drug Library, the ATR-FTIR Pharmaceuticals Library, the Georgia State Crime Laboratory Drug Library and the SWGDRUG Mass Spectral Library); it cannot detect substances below its limit of detection, reported as 3–4% w/w for fentanyl (citing Sherman et al., 2018), nor novel substances missing from the libraries. BTNX fentanyl strips were used on every sample to detect fentanyl and some analogues the maker says they cross-react with (butyrylfentanyl, acetylfentanyl, furanylfentanyl). FTIR approximate quantification was available but is not reported (PDF p. 6, 2. Material and methods, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The commonest composition of samples sold as heroin was caffeine (typically the most abundant component), a sugar alcohol (mannitol, xylitol or sorbitol) and strip-detected fentanyl (PDF p. 8, 3. Results, 2nd paragraph); other unexpected contents are listed as examples (PDF p. 9).

comparison.controls: None. Results are compared with what the client expected the sample to be ('match').
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not measured or not reported: who submitted samples (number of people, repeat submissions), the form of each sample by category (only that very few pills or liquids were tested), amounts, laboratory confirmation, and what clients did after receiving results.

outcomes.instruments: Fentanyl strip result (positive or negative) by expected drug category (Figure 1, PDF p. 16); match between the expected drug and FTIR findings by category (Figure 2, PDF p. 17); uptake of checking (per visit and per shift).
outcomes.validity_norms: The accuracy of the FTIR-plus-strip combination in this setting was not assessed; a second phase sending portions of samples for laboratory analysis to estimate sensitivity and specificity was under way (PDF pp. 6–7, 2. Material and methods, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Match' means any of the expected substance was detected; heroin matched if FTIR detected any diacetylmorphine or 6-monoacetylmorphine; samples of unknown expected content cannot match (Figure 2 legend, PDF p. 15). How a match was judged for samples expected to be fentanyl or carfentanil is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive counts and percentages, no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the technician recorded the client's expectation and the FTIR result before reading the strip (PDF p. 7, 2. Material and methods, 5th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Fentanyl strip positive (PDF pp. 7–9; Figure 1, PDF p. 16): expected heroin 822 of 907 (90.6%; editors' Wilson 95% CI 88.6–92.4, treating samples as independent); other opioids 66 of 99 (66.7%; 56.9–75.2); speed or crystal meth 15 of 256 (5.9%; 3.6–9.4); cocaine or crack 3 of 140 (2.1%; 0.7–6.1); 'psychedelic' 0 of 141; benzodiazepines 0 of 12; miscellaneous 0 of 16; unknown 30 of 143 (21.0%; 15.1–28.4). Match with expectation (Figure 2, PDF p. 17): heroin 160 of 907 (17.6%; 15.3–20.3); other opioids 26 of 99 (26.3%; 18.6–35.7); speed or crystal meth 225 of 256 (87.9%); cocaine or crack 128 of 140 (91.4%); 'psychedelic' 122 of 141 (86.5%). Editors' calculation: 936 of 1,714 samples (54.6%) strip-positive overall; with the 9 samples without a strip result removed from the denominators, heroin 822 of 905 (90.8%). The paper gives no intervals or tests; intervals that treat samples as independent are too narrow if samples cluster by person or batch.
analysis.preregistration_detail: University of British Columbia research ethics approval (PDF p. 5); no protocol or registration mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: FTIR quantification was available but not reported (PDF p. 6). The number of pills and liquids is not given (PDF p. 9). The comparison of uptake with an earlier strip-only project rests on a conference presentation (PDF p. 9).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 1,714 samples brought by a self-selected group of supervised-consumption clients, 90.6% of samples sold as heroin were fentanyl-positive by strip, and FTIR found heroin in 17.6% of them; most stimulant samples contained the expected drug, and 5.9% (speed or crystal meth) and 2.1% (cocaine or crack) were fentanyl-positive; no sample in the 'psychedelic', benzodiazepine or miscellaneous groups was fentanyl-positive. Nothing was confirmed by a laboratory, and nothing was recorded about what clients did with their results.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion says the results demonstrated that much of the downtown Vancouver opioid market, in particular the heroin market, has been adulterated or entirely supplanted by fentanyl (PDF p. 10), although the Results call the samples convenience samples not necessarily representative of the market (PDF p. 7). The Results describe utilization as significantly higher with FTIR plus strips than with strips alone, comparing 24 checks per six-hour shift with 5 per 18-hour shift in an earlier project cited from a conference presentation, with no statistical test and no common period (PDF p. 9). The abstract's conclusion of feasibility for identifying samples with unexpected substances is supported for feasibility, not for accuracy, which was not checked. The conclusion that the study has shown some potential for drug checking to lessen the public health emergency (PDF p. 10) rests on no outcome data; behavioural change was explicitly outside the study's scope (PDF p. 10).

timeline.event: Lysyshyn (2017), a conference presentation evaluating a fentanyl drug checking program for clients of a supervised injection site, cited for an earlier strip-only project at one of the two sites (an average of five checks per 18-hour shift; PDF p. 9). Not read.

Karamouzian et al. (2018), with M. Lysyshyn as a co-author and a near-identical title: strip-only fentanyl checking at Insite, a Vancouver supervised injection facility, 7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017; 1121 of 1411 checks fentanyl-positive, 939 (84.1%) of positive checks of client-reported heroin, with stated intentions to reduce the dose recorded (card sc_karamouzian_2018). This paper does not name its two sites, so the overlap of setting is likely but not stated.

McGowan et al. (2018), cited as showing that little is known about drug checking in the fentanyl epidemic (PDF p. 5); a review of whether enough was known to promote fentanyl self-testing outside supervised settings (card sc_mcgowan_2018).
This study (accepted manuscript; received 9 April, accepted 18 June 2018).

Laing et al. (2021): later BCCSU drug checking at eight harm-reduction sites in Vancouver and Surrey, October 2018 to January 2020, with FTIR, strips and confirmatory laboratory testing of a convenience subset; benzodiazepine strips and FTIR missed many novel benzodiazepines (card sc_laing_2021).

replication.where_it_stands: High fentanyl positivity in opioid samples checked at Vancouver supervised-consumption services is reported both by this pilot and by the earlier strip-only Insite service (Karamouzian et al., 2018); both are convenience samples tested without laboratory confirmation in the periods reported, so they agree but are not independent of the setting. Later work from the same centre added confirmatory testing (Laing et al., 2021). What people did with results is not answered here; Karamouzian et al. (2018) recorded stated intentions only.

funding.funder: The pilot program was supported by the City of Vancouver, the BC Ministry of Health, the BC Ministry of Mental Health and Addictions, and Vancouver Coastal Health; the research was undertaken in part with funding from the Canada Research Chairs program through a Tier 1 Canada Research Chair in Inner City Medicine, which supports Dr. Evan Wood (PDF p. 11, Role of the Funding Source).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (PDF p. 11, Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the BC Centre on Substance Use, the University of British Columbia and Vancouver Coastal Health (PDF p. 2), the organizations that ran the pilot, so the programme is evaluated by its operators. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Laboratory confirmation (for example LC–MS) of all checked samples or a random sample of them, with submissions linked to anonymous person codes so that repeat samples are identified, and with recorded actions after results (not using, using less, not using alone) and later overdose outcomes, compared with clients who did not check.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Clients of two supervised consumption services: a fair frame for what these clients bring, not for the city's drug market (authors' statement).
Convenience samples from self-selected clients, during limited service hours.
1,714 samples, with 99 to 907 in the main opioid and stimulant categories; the benzodiazepine (12) and miscellaneous (16) groups are small and the 'psychedelic' group is mixed.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Sites, period, technology and procedure are described; the number of people, repeat submissions and sample forms by category are not reported.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 1,705 of 1,714 samples have a strip result; all have an FTIR result reported by category.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: FTIR and fentanyl strips are screening methods: FTIR misses low concentrations (so heroin below its limit counts as no match) and the strips' accuracy here is unknown; no laboratory confirmation.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same two-stage protocol by trained technicians for every sample, but strips were read knowing the FTIR result, and the match rule for fentanyl-expected samples is not stated.
Counts and percentages recompute, but there are no intervals, clustering by person is ignored, the figure cross-references are swapped and the uptake figures do not reconcile.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a description of what this self-selected group of supervised-consumption clients brought for checking, the counts are clear and internally consistent; as an estimate of what people in Vancouver were buying, the risk of bias is high because of convenience sampling, possible repeat submissions and unconfirmed screening methods. Citable for: in a Vancouver drug-checking pilot in 2017–2018, about 9 in 10 samples sold as heroin tested positive for fentanyl by strip and FTIR found heroin in fewer than 1 in 5; about 1 in 17 speed or crystal meth samples and about 1 in 50 cocaine samples tested positive for fentanyl; no 'psychedelic' samples did. Not citable for: market-wide prevalence, accuracy of the methods, pills, or any effect of checking on behaviour or overdose.

key_findings.finding: Between 31 October 2017 and 30 April 2018, 1,714 samples were checked at two supervised consumption services in downtown Vancouver; the sites had 69,733 visits in the period, checking was offered two days a week in six-hour shifts at each site, and the authors give uptake as less than 2% of visits. The samples were convenience samples from a self-selected subset of clients and are not necessarily representative of the broader market.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 1,714 samples over 69,733 visits is 2.5%; the stated 'less than 2%' holds only if some visits contributed more than one sample, which is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Of 907 samples sold as heroin, FTIR found heroin (any diacetylmorphine or 6-monoacetylmorphine) in 160 (17.6%), and 822 (90.6%) tested positive for fentanyl by strip. The commonest make-up of these samples was caffeine (typically the main component), a sugar alcohol such as mannitol, xylitol or sorbitol, and strip-detected fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 2nd paragraph (begins PDF p. 7); Figures 1–2 data tables (PDF pp. 16–17); also Abstract › Results and Highlights (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Of 99 samples sold as other opioids (the text lists carfentanil, fentanyl, hydromorphone, morphine and oxycodone; the figure legend adds methadone, oxycodone/paracetamol and U-44770), 26 (26.3%) contained the expected substance and 66 (66.7%) tested positive for fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 2nd paragraph (continued, PDF p. 8); Figure legends (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Stimulants (396 samples): 225 of 256 samples sold as speed or crystal meth (87.9%) contained amphetamine or methamphetamine and 15 (5.9%) tested positive for fentanyl; 128 of 140 samples sold as cocaine or crack (91.4%) contained cocaine and 3 (2.1%) tested positive for fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 3rd paragraph; also Abstract › Results (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Of 141 samples loosely grouped as 'psychedelic' (for example DMT, GHB, ketamine, LSD, MDMA, MDA, mushroom extract, 4-MMC, DiPT, 5-MeO-DiPT), 122 (86.5%) contained some of the expected substance and none tested positive for fentanyl; none of 12 benzodiazepine samples (alprazolam, etizolam, lorazepam) or 16 miscellaneous samples (for example cannabis extract, caffeine) tested positive; of 143 samples whose expected content was unknown or not stated, 30 (21.0%) tested positive.
key_findings.locator: 3. Results, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 8) and 5th paragraph (PDF p. 9)

key_findings.finding: The vast majority of samples were powders and very few pills or liquids were tested (no number given); the authors suggest this may reflect clients' limited knowledge of possible counterfeit pills or market availability.

Unexpected substances other than fentanyl (examples): a sample sold as MDMA was N-ethylbuphedrone, a cathinone; one heroin sample contained oxazepam; a methamphetamine sample was ketamine; a heroin sample was DMT; cocaine was cut with ground pumice; several heroin samples were mainly feldspar dust or plaster with no heroin detected.

Strip results by category, including samples without a strip result (Figure 1 data table): heroin 822 positive, 83 negative, 2 not tested; other opioids 66, 33, 0; 'psychedelic' 0, 139, 2; amphetamines 15, 240, 1; cocaine 3, 136, 1; unknown 30, 110, 3. Match results (Figure 2 data table): heroin 160 true, 747 false; other opioids 26, 73; 'psychedelic' 122, 19; amphetamines 225, 31; cocaine 128, 12.
key_findings.locator: Figure 1 and Figure 2, data tables printed under the charts

key_findings.finding: Methods and their limits: FTIR cannot detect substances below its limit of detection (reported as 3–4% w/w for fentanyl) or novel substances absent from its libraries; fentanyl strips were therefore used on all samples and fentanyl positivity was generally ascertained by strip; FTIR quantification is not reported; gas chromatography–mass spectrometry and HPLC were not feasible with the pilot's funding; a second phase was sending sample portions for laboratory analysis to validate the method's sensitivity and specificity.

Uptake: an average of 24 FTIR-plus-strip checks per six-hour shift, against an average of five checks per 18-hour shift in an earlier strip-only project at one of the sites; clients reportedly wanted the fuller information FTIR gives (no data shown).
key_findings.note: No statistical test, no common period and different shift lengths, although the text calls the difference significant. Editors' calculation: 1,714 samples over about 26 weeks at four shifts a week (about 103 shifts) is about 17 per shift; 24 per shift implies about 71 shifts; the number of shifts run is not reported.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that laboratory confirmation (for example HPLC–mass spectrometry) was lacking, and that interest in checking among sub-populations, motivations for using the service, and resulting behavioural change were outside the study's scope.

reporting_issues.issue: The text's figure cross-references are swapped: it cites Figure 1 for the heroin match result and Figure 2 for fentanyl positivity, but Figure 1 shows strip results and Figure 2 shows matches with expectation (legends, PDF p. 15; figures, PDF pp. 16–17).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; anchors should name Figure 1 for fentanyl strips and Figure 2 for matches.

reporting_issues.issue: Uptake is given as less than 2% of 69,733 visits, but 1,714 samples are 2.5% of visits (editors' calculation); this reconciles only if some visits contributed more than one sample, which is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite uptake as about 2% to 2.5% of visits, or as 1,714 samples in 69,733 visits.

reporting_issues.issue: The average of 24 checks per six-hour shift does not fit 1,714 samples over about 26 weeks at two days a week at each of two sites (about 103 shifts, about 17 checks per shift; editors' calculation); the number of shifts actually run is not reported. The comparison with 5 checks per 18-hour shift is called significant without a test.
reporting_issues.consequence: The utilization comparison cannot be cited as a measured or significant difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The Abstract and Methods date the start to November 2017 (PDF pp. 3, 5); the Results date it from 31 October 2017 (PDF p. 7).

Fentanyl percentages use whole category totals as denominators although 9 samples had no strip result (for example 822 of 907 = 90.6%; 822 of 905 tested = 90.8%, editors' calculation); the text says the strip could not be used, while Figure 1 labels these samples as declined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the percentages change by less than half a point.

reporting_issues.issue: Heroin 'match' rests on FTIR detection, which misses substances below its limit of detection (given only for fentanyl, 3–4% w/w); samples containing heroin below that limit would be counted as not matching.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 17.6% is the share of 'heroin' samples in which FTIR detected heroin, a lower bound for the share containing any heroin.

reporting_issues.issue: How a 'match' was judged for samples expected to be fentanyl or carfentanil (in the other-opioid group) is not stated, and the 'psychedelic' group mixes non-psychedelic drugs (GHB, ketamine, 4-MMC) with MDMA and others, whose results are not given separately.
reporting_issues.consequence: The other-opioid match rate (26.3%) is hard to interpret, and the paper gives no MDMA-specific result.

verification.source_read: PDF (accepted manuscript, Elsevier 'Accepted Manuscript', DAD 7050; received 9 April 2018, revised 17 June 2018, accepted 18 June 2018), PDF pp. 1–17 (all pages: text pp. 3–11, references pp. 12–14, figure legends p. 15, Figures 1–2 with their data tables pp. 16–17; every number checked on the rendered pages; no supplement). Not the version of record (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 190, 242–245): anchors give the manuscript's PDF pages, which differ from the published pages.
